children.value: The methods of the previous section rarely reach an application in raw form. They arrive packaged inside libraries, search engines, and databases that also handle storage, updates, and scale. This section follows one realistic query through four widely used systems: the FAISS library, the Lucene library, the OpenSearch engine, and the pgvector extension for PostgreSQL. We first look at how each system answers the vector part of the query, and then at how each one adds metadata filters and keyword search.

stored a title, an overview, a rating, and a year for every movie. We extend it with two text fields, the main actors and the genres, and with an embedding of the overview, computed by an embedding model as in
. With a model such as Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, every movie receives a vector with 1,024 dimensions. A user now types:
a mind-bending heist thriller with Leonardo DiCaprio, released after 2005, rated 7.5 or better
No single retrieval method covers this request. Each part of it asks for a different kind of match:
vector search on the overview embedding

describes a thief who steals secrets by entering the dreams of his targets. It contains neither “mind-bending” nor “heist”, so BM25 on the overview would miss it. An embedding does better, but not well enough on its own: among 10,000 movies embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the vector search alone ranks Inception only 138th, behind movies whose overviews match “heist thriller” more literally. Names behave the other way round. An embedding blurs “Leonardo DiCaprio” into a region of similar actors, while BM25 matches the name exactly. The year and the rating are not matters of degree at all: a movie from 2001 must not appear, however similar it is. Each ingredient matters. The filters on year and rating lift Inception to second place among the 261 admitted movies, and fusing the vector ranking with BM25 on the actors puts it first. The rest of this section builds this query step by step: first the vector search, then the filters and the keyword search.
FAISS: a library of vector indexes

children.label: FAISS: a library of vector indexes

children.value: (Facebook AI Similarity Search), developed at Meta, is a C++ library with Python bindings that runs on CPUs and GPUs. It implements all methods of the previous section and lets us combine them freely through index type strings. FAISS stores only vectors and their integer identifiers. The titles, the actors, and the years stay in the application’s own data store, and the application maps the returned identifiers back to movies.

import faiss
import numpy as np

# 1. Movie embeddings (one row per movie) and their movie ids
X = np.load("overview_embeddings.npy").astype("float32")   # shape (n, 1024)
ids = np.load("movie_ids.npy").astype("int64")
faiss.normalize_L2(X)               # unit length: inner product = cosine

# 2. Build an IVF index with PQ codes (lever 3 + lever 2)
index = faiss.index_factory(1024, "IVF256,PQ64", faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
index.train(X)                      # k-means for the centers and the codebooks
index.add_with_ids(X, ids)

# 3. Search: embed the query and probe 16 of the 256 lists
q = embed("a mind-bending heist thriller").reshape(1, -1)
faiss.normalize_L2(q)
index.nprobe = 16
scores, movie_ids = index.search(q, 10)
Step 1 normalizes the vectors, so that the inner product equals the cosine similarity. Step 2 builds the composite index of the previous section:
runs k-means to find the 256 centers of the inverted file and the codebooks of the product quantizer, and
encodes every vector into 64 one-byte codes. Step 3 sets the tuning knob

Lucene: vectors next to the inverted index

children.label: Lucene: vectors next to the inverted index

children.value: stores vectors as one more field type of a document. The document of
next to its text and numeric fields:

Lucene builds an HNSW graph for the vector field of every segment. A query searches the graph of each segment and merges the per-segment results, the same scatter-gather pattern as for text queries. Because segments are merged in the background, their graphs must be merged as well, which makes indexing vectors considerably more expensive than indexing text. Lucene reports cosine similarity as a score in

children.html: [0,1][0, 1][0,1]
(1+cos⁡)/2(1 + \cos)/2(1+cos)/2

searches only the leading 256 components of a Matryoshka embedding. The refine step is plain SQL: an inner query retrieves candidates through a compact index, and an outer query reorders them by the full vectors.

-- Binary codes for the candidate search, full vectors for the final order
CREATE INDEX ON movies
  USING hnsw ((binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(1024)) bit_hamming_ops);

SELECT title FROM (
  SELECT title, embedding FROM movies
  ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(1024)
           <~> binary_quantize('[0.021, ...]'::vector)
  LIMIT 100                                     -- k' = 100 candidates
) AS candidates
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]'
LIMIT 10;
The four systems expose the levers of the previous section in different ways:
PCA stage in the index string
The vector query finds movies with mind-bending heist plots, but it ignores the rest of the request. We now add the filters on year and rating and the keyword part for the actor and the genre.
Combining a filter with a vector search is harder than it looks, because the ANN index knows nothing about the metadata. There are three strategies.

applies the metadata condition first and then compares the query exactly with the vectors that pass. The result is exact, and the cost depends on how many vectors pass. A selective filter makes this cheap: if a filter admits 0.01% of the billion vectors of the previous section, an exact scan over the 100,000 survivors reads only 300 MB. A mild filter makes it expensive, because the scan over the survivors approaches a full scan.
runs the ANN search first and discards the results that fail the filter. This keeps the index intact, but it can return too few results. With HNSW and the default

of 40, a pgvector index scan delivers about 40 candidates. If the filter matches 10% of the rows, only about 4 of them survive, even if the query asked for 10. A fixed over-fetch, retrieving more candidates than requested, helps only if we guess the selectivity right. The robust form treats the index as a
in order of increasing distance, like the incremental nearest-neighbor algorithm of
: the filter consumes candidates from the stream until

children.html: kkk

children.value: of them pass. HNSW suits this form well. Its search already maintains a queue of candidates, and continuing the search simply extends the queue into regions further away from the query. pgvector’s iterative index scans work this way.
Post-filtering can silently return too few results

If a query asks for the ten nearest neighbors and then removes those failing a selective filter, the final list may contain far fewer than ten items, or be empty, even though many matching documents exist deeper in the ranking. Over-fetch a larger candidate set before filtering, and verify that enough results survive.

evaluates the filter first, for example as a bitmap over all document ids, and passes it to the ANN search, which only accepts admitted documents as results. This fits the inverted file particularly well. An IVF search with PQ codes scans the lists of the probed centers entry by entry anyway; checking each entry against the bitmap costs one bit lookup and lets the scan skip the distance computation for every non-admitted vector. The search itself does not change, only its result is restricted. In the billion-vector example with 16 of 4,096 lists probed, the scan visits about 3.9 million codes. If the filter admits 1% of the collection, about 39,000 of these are admitted, far more than needed for a top 10.

The limit lies in very selective filters. If the filter admits only 0.001% of the collection, the probed lists contain about 39 admitted vectors, and the ten best of them may be poor matches, because the good admitted matches lie in lists that were not probed. Probing more lists helps, but at this selectivity the 10,000 admitted vectors fit into an exact scan of 30 MB, which is both cheaper and exact. Systems that filter during the search therefore choose per query: if only a few documents pass the filter, they skip the index and fall back to pre-filtering with an exact scan. Graph indexes can filter during the search as well, but they must still step through non-matching nodes, because these can lie on the path to a matching one. With a selective filter, most steps of the graph search are wasted.
Keyword search adds a second ranking.

FAISS has no metadata, so the application evaluates the filter on its own data and passes the admitted ids to the search. An

Lucene filters during the search. The filter is passed as the fourth argument of

. Lucene evaluates it per segment and searches the graph only for admitted documents. If fewer documents pass the filter than the query asks for, it runs an exact search instead, and if the graph search visits too many vectors without completing, it stops and switches to an exact search as well. The keyword part becomes ordinary BM25 clauses of a Boolean query:
Two details matter here. First, the filter belongs inside the vector query. Adding it only as a
clause of the Boolean query, next to an unfiltered

, runs the two parts independently: the vector query returns its top 50 over all movies, and the Boolean query intersects them with the filter. This is post-filtering, with all its risks. Second, a Boolean query adds the scores of its clauses. The vector clause contributes at most 1, while a BM25 clause for a rare name can contribute several points, so the keyword part tends to dominate. Lucene itself provides no rank fusion; applications either weight the clauses with boosts or run the two queries separately and fuse their rankings with RRF.
OpenSearch passes a filter inside the
clause to the engine, which then filters during the search in the same way as Lucene. For the keyword part, a
query runs its sub-queries separately, and a search pipeline fuses their results. Since version 2.19, the
of the hybrid query applies to both sub-queries. Instead of RRF, the pipeline can also use a

, which rescales the scores of each sub-query to a common range and then combines them with weights. This keeps more information than ranks alone, at the cost of choosing a normalization and the weights.
In SQL, the filter is an ordinary

clause. With an approximate index, PostgreSQL applies it after the index scan, which is post-filtering with the risk described above. Since version 0.8, pgvector’s iterative index scans continue through the index until enough rows pass the filter. The keyword part uses PostgreSQL’s full-text search from
, and the fusion is written in SQL:

-- 1. Filtered vector search; continue the index scan until enough rows pass
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

-- 2. Hybrid search: dense and sparse rankings, fused with RRF (k = 60)
WITH dense AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]') AS r
  FROM movies
  WHERE year > 2005 AND rating >= 7.5
  ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]'
  LIMIT 50
),
sparse AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC) AS r
  FROM movies, to_tsquery('(leonardo <-> dicaprio) | thriller') AS q
  WHERE tsv @@ q AND year > 2005 AND rating >= 7.5
  ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC
  LIMIT 50
)
SELECT m.title,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + d.r), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.r), 0) AS rrf
FROM dense d
FULL OUTER JOIN sparse s ON d.id = s.id
JOIN movies m ON m.id = COALESCE(d.id, s.id)
ORDER BY rrf DESC
LIMIT 10;

The four systems implement the same methods but serve different settings.
gives the most control over the index and the highest speed, including on GPUs, but it handles only vectors: filters, keyword search, storage, and updates remain the application’s job.
keeps vectors, text, and metadata in one index and filters during the search, which suits Java applications that embed their search.
adds distribution across many machines and a complete hybrid pipeline with filters and rank fusion, at the price of operating a cluster.

keeps vectors next to the relational data, with SQL filters, joins, and transactions, and suits collections that fit on a single database server. Dedicated vector databases, such as Milvus, Qdrant, and Weaviate, follow the same patterns, and several of them appear in the benchmark of the previous section.

Whatever the system, the query of this section needs the same three ingredients: an approximate vector search for the meaning, a keyword search for names and terms, and filters for the hard constraints. What differs is how much of the combination the system does for us.
